i-am-me asked me to post more about the various texts I have explored in my search for morals.

So the hippies, right, they gave me this book, Bhagavad-Gita, which, in the first few pages, references the Upanishads. You go back to the Upanishads, I like the Patrick Olivelle version, I think his name is, it's written for scholars and has lots of good footnotes. Some translations are skewed by the people who translate them to make it fit their religious purpose or whatever, but his is pretty good, I think.

Now the Upanishads reference the Vedas, which are even earlier texts, some of the earliest we are aware of, and these are very difficult to get through, as there's a lot of repetitive prayers and such.

The Upanishads explain the Vedas. Upanishads means hidden knowledge, and in ancient times this knowledge was verbally passed down between the priests, or brahmins, so they knew what the fuck they were talking about when they prayed.

The Upanishads explain everything. They explain how the sun is in your right eye and your breath is the wind and it gets rather trippy, but there's a lot of explanations in there about the nature of reality that really helped me very much so. I recommend Yajnavalka's conversation with his wives. There's a lot about how to act and what to do in various situations in both the Upanishads and the Vedas. The Upanishads are all, do this and you'll get a thousand cows and live a long life etcetera, much more direct than any Western religion I've found.

The symbol of Taoism, the white and black circle thingy, is made by planting a pole in the ground and measuring it's shadow at the same time of day for a year, then putting those measurements on a chart and swirling the chart into a circle. I guess it's about the balance of things, and keeping things in balance.
